blocks.p: Teo Thorne wanted to know everything, and he wanted to know it before supper.

He had attached himself to Sol on the second day, the way a gull attaches itself to a boat, and nothing Lyda said had detached him. He was waiting at the foot of the loft ladder in the mornings. He found reasons to be wherever Sol had been sent, and once there he worked twice as fast as Sol did and talked the whole time. What was the gravity on Ganymede? Had Sol ever seen Saturn from Titan, or was it true you couldn’t? How many crossings had he made? What did stasis feel like, if you were awake enough to notice? Was it true that in Sion the buildings were so tall they had weather at the top?

And he called him Sol. He had done it from the first hour, without asking, the way he did everything. No one had called Sol by his first name in all the time he could remember except a dying man and a dockworker, and now a boy of sixteen shouted it across the wharf a dozen times a day as if it were the most ordinary word in the world.

“You’ve got more grey than when you came,” Teo said one afternoon, three weeks after the visit to the doctor. They were in the long dye shed below Sol’s loft, restacking bales of dried inkreed for the next ship. “Lyda says it’s because you’re old. I said everybody’s old. She said, not like that.”
“She’s right.”
“Lucan says you’re getting a year older every month.” Teo heaved a bale up onto the stack and turned around, interested. “Does it hurt?”

Sol considered it honestly. His knees hurt, kneeling. His back hurt in the mornings until he had walked the length of the wharf, and he no longer blamed it all on Philippa. Lucan had measured him three times more and written down what he found, and the grey above Sol’s ears had spread back toward the crown, and the line beside his left eye had found a companion.
“Not the way you’d think,” he said.

“I’d like to be old,” Teo said. “Properly. Like Jory. I’d like to have done so many things my face can’t hold them all.” He swung himself up the stack, two bales at a time, the way Lyda had told him a hundred times not to, and sat at the top with his legs hanging. “Why are you on the relay, anyway? Lyda won’t say.”
“I said a word I wasn’t supposed to.”
“What word?”

Sol looked up at him. The boy’s face was bright and open and entirely without fear, and at his temple, under the skin, sat the coin that went home to Sion every moment of every day. Sol did not know what it could carry. He did not know what Teo would do with the word if he had it, or who would be standing nearby when he did.
“Not yet,” he said.
Teo made a face, and then grinned, as if not yet were a promise. “Weir’s coming,” he said, looking past Sol at the open river doors. “Be nice to Weir. Everyone’s nice to Weir.”

Ansel Weir came along the wharf in the grey coat of the chapel with a slate under his arm. He was a round, soft-spoken man with a careful face that was beginning, at the jowls, to slip. He kept the chapel’s registry and the queue for its Renewal Font, and Sol had learned in three weeks what that meant on Philippa. The Font had been down since the spring, and down more often than up for six years before that. When the parts came, the queue would decide who went under it first and who waited another year getting older, and the queue was Weir’s. People brought him fish. People mended his roof. People told him things.
He had been by twice already, asking after the new hand.
“Remember the Mountain,” he said pleasantly from the doorway.
The answer was ready in Sol’s mouth; he had said it more often than his own name. He could not make it come out.
“And forget the tears,” Teo called down brightly from the top of the stack.
“Teo.” Weir smiled up at him. “Your new man doesn’t answer the greeting.”
“He’s from the inner colonies. They’re all stuck up.”

“Are they.” Weir looked at Sol. His eyes were mild and pale and they did not move quickly, but they did not miss much. “The chapel likes every soul on the river in its registry. I don’t believe I have yours.”
“Sol.”
“Just Sol.”
“Just Sol.”

Weir touched his temple, lightly, and his eyes went for a moment to the corner of his sight. Then he looked up at the boy on the bales. “Careful up there. You know how you are.” He turned to go, and turned back. “Tell your sister the Font parts are on the Kestrel’s next run from Plenty. I’ll be by.”
He went away along the wharf.

“He means he’ll be by to make sure he’s first,” Teo said. “He hasn’t been under in six years. Other worlds kept getting the parts. He counts his grey hairs.” He stood up on top of the stack, balancing, arms out, a pilot on a gantry. “Watch. I can walk the whole top row without...”
He stopped.

He was standing very still, with his arms still out. His face had changed. It had gone blank and inward, as if he were listening for something a long way off, and Sol had seen that look once before, over a spice stall in the Bounty Market, and his heart went cold.
“Sol,” Teo said, in a small careful voice that did not sound like his. “It’s going bright.”

He began to climb down. He did it deliberately, carefully, the way a person does a thing he has been taught to do and has practiced: turning, finding the edge of the bale below with his foot, lowering himself. He got halfway.
Then a cry tore out of him, thin and wordless, and he stiffened, and fell.

On Mars a man went down slowly, as if he were lying down to sleep. On Philippa there was no slowness in it. Teo came off the bales the way a sack comes off a hoist, rigid, with his arms locked against his chest and his back arched, and Sol had no time to think. He stepped in and caught the boy across the chest and shoulders, and the weight of him and the weight of the world together took them both straight down onto the boards. Sol’s knee struck the floor and something in it shouted. Teo’s head missed the planks by the width of Sol’s forearm.
Then the jerking began.

Sol got out from under him. He pulled his own coat off and folded it and slid it under the boy’s head, as he had once slid his robe under an old man’s on Martian tiles. He pushed the loose bales back out of reach of the flailing arms. Clear the space. Don’t hold him down. Nothing in his mouth. He knelt on his aching knee and put his hand flat on the floor beside the boy’s head, not touching him, only there.
Note the time.

He had no clock. He counted. Teo’s face had gone dusky around the lips; he was not breathing, and then he was, in great snoring pulls through his teeth. His whole body jerked in a rhythm that seemed to come from somewhere outside him, from the boards, from the river beneath the boards, and on each jerk the heavy gravity slammed his heels and elbows down again, so that it was nothing like the old man on Mars, thrown into the air and floating. Here the world held him down hard and shook him.
The door from the counting house banged open.
Lyda came in at a run, and saw, and Sol watched what she did, and understood everything.

She did not come to her brother. She went first to the great river doors, standing open on the wharf and the slow brown water and anyone who might be passing in a boat, and she put her shoulder to the first door and dragged it shut along its rail, and then the second, so that the shed went dim. Only then did she come and drop to her knees on Teo’s other side.
Her hands knew where to go. They went to his collar and loosened it. They went to his hip and his shoulder and waited there, ready, not pressing. Her lips were moving. She was counting too.
“Ninety,” she said under her breath. “He’s usually two minutes. Come on, Teo. Come on.”

It was two minutes, near enough. The jerks slowed and came further apart, and stopped. Lyda turned him onto his side in one smooth movement, the way you would turn a sleeper, and tipped his chin, and a thread of blood and spit ran out of his mouth onto Sol’s coat. He lay there hauling in breath after breath, slow and ragged, with the whites of his eyes showing under the lids.

Lyda sat back on her heels. Her face was white and perfectly composed. She had done this before. She had done it, Sol thought, more times than she could count; and she had done it alone, every time, with the doors shut.
Teo began to speak.

It was barely a voice, a slur of breath. Lyda’s hand moved toward his mouth. Sol saw it move and saw it stop, an inch from the boy’s lips, as if it had been doing this for years without being asked and had only now been asked.
“He makes me lie down,” Teo said, “in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.” A long breath. “He restores my soul.”
Lyda did not move. She was looking at her brother with an expression Sol had never seen on any face in Sion: a fear so old and so worn that it had become a kind of tenderness.
“He leads me in paths...” Teo’s voice failed. His lips went on moving.
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,” Sol said quietly, “I will fear no evil, for you are with me.”
Lyda’s head came up.
She looked at him across her brother’s body as if he had reached into her house and taken something out of a locked drawer that no one in the worlds was supposed to know was there.
“You know it,” she said.
Someone knocked on the side door.
“Lyda?” Ansel Weir’s mild voice. “Lyda, are you in there? I heard someone cry out.”

For one moment she did not move at all. Then she was on her feet and wiping her hands on her trousers, and her face, when she reached the door, had nothing in it but impatience. She opened it a hand’s width and stood in the gap.
“Teo fell off the bales,” she said. “Knocked the wind out of himself. He’s fine.”
“I heard him cry out.”
“You’d cry out too.”

Weir did not try to look past her. He did not have to. From where he stood, through the gap, Sol knew he could see a slice of the dim shed: a stranger who did not answer the greeting, kneeling on the floor, and a boy lying on his side on a folded coat, quite still, in the position they taught at every chapel school on every world.
“He has a great many falls, your brother,” Weir said gently. “Over the years. Fainting. Falling.”
“He’s sixteen. He’s made of elbows.”

“Of course.” A pause. “I’ll pray for his health. And I’ll come back about your man’s name, Lyda. Every soul on the river belongs in the registry. You know that.” Another pause, softer. “The Font parts on the Kestrel. You’ll let me know when she’s in.”
“I always do.”
She shut the door. She stood with her palm flat against it and her forehead almost touching the wood. She stayed like that a long time.

They carried Teo up to the loft between them. He was heavy and limp and he mumbled when they moved him, and Philippa pulled at all three of them on the ladder, and Sol’s knee shouted on every rung. They laid him on Sol’s cot. He was asleep almost at once, the deep blank sleep that comes after, with his mouth open and his hair stuck to his forehead and a bruise already coming up on one cheekbone. Lyda drew the blanket over him and sat on the floor beside the cot with her back against the wall. Sol sat on the stained boards across from her. The lamp burned between them.

“He was four,” she said at last. “The first time. In his bed, in the night. Our mother was two years gone and our father was on a crossing. I was twenty-three. I knew what it was. Every child on this river sat through the chapel films at school. The stiffening, the cry, the wardens coming, the mothers covering their children’s ears.” She did not look at him. “I sat on the floor with him and I knew exactly what they’d do, and when he started talking afterward I put my hand over his mouth so the neighbors wouldn’t hear. I’ve been doing it for twelve years.”
“Did your father know?”
“I told him it was fainting. He believed me. He wanted to.” She was quiet a moment. “Then he went down with the Marten when Teo was six, and there was no one to tell.”
“And the Halo,” Sol said.

“He wanted to fly. Pilots need a Halo for the crossings. I had him haloed at nine.” Her voice was very even. “I knew the couch would read him as noise. But out here it reads everyone as noise. The Halo doesn’t tell, Bishop. Only people tell. So I keep him away from people.” She looked up then, for the first time. “I’ve stalled his clearance for a year. Lucan keeps asking me to bring him in. I tell him Teo’s grown out of the fainting.”
“Lucan has reported no one in thirty-one years. He told me so.”
“And you believe him.”
“Yes.”
“You believe a great many people,” Lyda said, “for a man who used to sign them away.”
He took it. It was true.

“Weir has wondered for years,” she said. “Not enough to do anything. Not enough to risk his place in the queue by being wrong about a Thorne. And then a man nobody knows comes off one of my ships, a man who won’t say Remember the Mountain, and Weir has a reason to come to my door twice a week.” She did not say it cruelly. She said it the way she read a figure off a ledger. “You did that.”
“Yes,” Sol said. “I’ll go. There’s a ship at the end of the week.”

“And Weir writes down that the stranger left in a hurry the week my brother fell off a bale.” She shook her head. “No. You’ll stay, and you’ll answer the greeting, if it kills you, and I’ll see to Weir. The Font parts come in my hold. He’s waited six years. He’ll trade a great deal to be first under it.” Her mouth tightened. “Everyone on this river has something they’d sell to be first into that Font. That’s what it’s for.”
Teo stirred on the cot and muttered and was still. Lyda watched him until his breathing evened again.

“What is it?” she said quietly. “What he says. He’s said things like it since he was four. Never the same twice, quite. I thought it was nonsense the sickness made. Then you sat there and finished it.”
“It’s a song,” Sol said. “A very old one. The man in the market said it to me, before they took him. The people at Jory’s say it.”
“Jory’s.” She did not ask. She had, he thought, been carefully not asking about Jory’s for years. “What’s it about?”
“A shepherd.”
“A shepherd.” Something that was almost a laugh went out of her. “On a world where nobody has ever seen a sheep.”
“I’ve never seen one either.”
“Then what good is it?”
He thought about the white cell on Serenity, and the net loft, and the boy on the floor of the shed with his sister’s hand stopped an inch from his mouth.
“It says that even in the valley of the shadow of death,” he said, “you don’t have to be afraid. Because someone is with you.”
“Who?”
“I’m finding out.”

She looked at him across the lamp for a long time. He did not know what she saw. He knew what Lucan’s mirror had shown him that week: a man who might have been forty-one or forty-two, with grey at the temples and lines at the eyes and a stiffness in the way he sat on the floor that he could no longer blame on the gravity.
“You look older than when you came,” she said.
“I am.”
She got up. She stood a moment with her hand on the ladder rail, looking at her brother.

“He wakes confused,” she said. “He’s frightened if no one’s there. Usually it’s me.” She hesitated, and it was the first time Sol had seen her hesitate over anything. “I need to go and find Weir before he finds anyone else. Will you sit with him?”
“Yes.”
“Thank you,” Lyda said.
“Don’t,” said Sol.
She stopped on the top rung and looked at him. Then something moved at the corner of her mouth, and this time it was nearly a smile, and she went down the ladder and was gone.

When she had been gone a while, the voice came, low and crackling, almost tender. You’ll sign for this one too. You brought them to his door. You’ll sign for him too. Sol looked at the sleeping boy and said the name under his breath, so softly that it would not wake him, and the voice broke into static and fell away.
Teo woke a little after midnight.

He woke the way they all woke, Sol thought, the way he himself had woken on the floor of the packet: slowly, from a long way down, not knowing for a while where he was. His eyes moved over the rafters and the round window and the lamp, and found Sol, and stopped.
“Sol?” His voice was thick. He touched his bitten tongue against his teeth and winced. “Did I... I did. Didn’t I.”
“Yes.”
“Where’s Lyda?”
“Seeing to something. She’ll be back.”
Teo lay still. Then he said, very quietly, without any of his brightness, “I said something. After. I always say something. She never tells me what.”
Sol looked at him: sixteen, bruised, frightened, with a coin in his temple that went home to Sion and a song in him that had never come from there.
“You said, He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul.”
Teo said it over to himself, silently, his lips moving. Something came into his face that was not fear.
“Who’s he?” he said.
Under the cot, in the dark, in a travel case from Concord, lay a grey notebook with a page in it that Sol had not yet turned.
“I don’t know yet,” Sol said. “But I know where to look.”
